sources.title: Soaring Gas Prices Making It Hard For Commuters To Get To Work
sources.snippet: # Soaring Gas Prices Making It Hard For Commuters To Get To Work. Skyrocketing fuel prices are inflicting pain at the pump as American commuters search for ways to afford gas—like pawning and selling personal belongings—just so they can get to work. Millions of Americans are starting their workday with a financial gut punch as spiking fuel prices inflict pain at the gas pump. The growing financial strain is quietly reshaping how Americans think about work, where they live and whether their jobs are still worth the commute. Crushing already-stretched household budgets, commuters are resorting to desperate steps to fill their tanks, like pawning personal belongings for quick cash to fill their tanks, get to work and keep their jobs. Workers who accepted return-to-office mandates after years of remote work are discovering that the cost of commuting can wipe out the financial benefit of raises. According to economists at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, rising gas prices hit workers particularly hard because fuel costs consume a larger percentage of lower-and middle-income household budgets.
sources.content: Millions of Americans are starting their workday with a financial gut punch as spiking fuel prices inflict pain at the gas pump. Ordinary commutes are turning into budget-breaking expenses, especially for workers who have little choice but to drive. The growing financial strain is quietly reshaping how Americans think about work, where they live and whether their jobs are still worth the commute. Crushing already-stretched household budgets, commuters are resorting to desperate steps to fill their tanks, like pawning personal belongings for quick cash to fill their tanks, get to work and keep their jobs. Commuters Are Slashing Their Budgets Experts often tell consumers to drive less, cut expenses or pick up a side hustle. But workers in parts of Los Angeles and San Francisco—already facing $8-a-gallon gas prices—see those solutions are cold comfort. Still, in many households, workers are scaling back grocery spending, travel, entertainment and discretionary purchases just to cover transportation costs. Others are dipping into savings, taking on side gigs or cutting essentials to offset expenses. Families with multiple commuters are particularly vulnerable, as is Gen Z who have little financial cushion. Even before the fuel crisis, data from Invoice Home shows that 48% of Gen Z was already planning to stop dining out this year to keep up with rising costs, 26% say they’re cutting back on groceries and other essential household goods, 31% plan to get a second job in this year and 32% say they will opt for generic brands over name brands to stretch their budgets. Financial experts recommend revisiting monthly budgets immediately rather than waiting for prices to stabilize. Small adjustments made early can prevent larger financial problems later, including consolidating errands into fewer trips, carpooling when possible or reducing unnecessary driving. Reactionary Tactics Commuters Are Using To Cope But budgeting alone has limits. For workers already living paycheck to paycheck, there may not be enough flexibility left to absorb higher fuel bills without larger life changes. Frustrated commuters are finding creative ways to reduce the financial hit. Some are negotiating compressed workweeks to reduce commuting days. Others are asking employers for transit stipends, hybrid schedules or flexible hours that avoid traffic congestion and reduce fuel consumption. Renita Parker, who oversees more than 75 EZCorp’s stores across Houston, told me she’s seeing firsthand a notable surge in customers pawning or selling their personal belongings into quick cash to fill their tanks and make it to work each week. “We recently had a customer come in to pawn items for extra gas money just to get through the week—even though he had just gotten paid that day,” Parker says. “We’ve also seen customers on fixed incomes who need extra money for groceries because of rising costs. This time of year especially, parents and students are pawning and selling items for extra cash for prom dresses, tuxedos and graduation gifts.” Parker said gold and silver jewelry remain among the most commonly pawned or sold items, along with premium sneakers and handbags ranging from vintage pieces to luxury brands. Electronics such as smartphones, laptops, smartwatches and gaming systems are also in high demand. Even everyday household items—including coffee makers, crockpots and blenders—are showing up at pawn counters. Other recently pawned items include sunglasses, golf clubs, tools and musical instruments. “Paychecks are being stretched especially thin by rising gas and grocery prices,” Parker adds. “People are exploring financing options that may be new to them, like visiting their local pawn store. We welcome them and want them to know our stores can provide help without judgment or the typical financial hurdles.” With prices unlikely to ease anytime soon, selling and pawning have become a practical, low-effort way for people to supplement between paychecks. explanation.text: Gas prices have increased to the point that many commuters are finding it financially challenging to afford their daily travel to work.

The thread mentions a call for improved public transportation as a solution to the high cost of commuting due to soaring fuel prices.
